aliases: consciousness in a small language model
projects.markdown:
I trained a small language model (SLM) of about 100 million parameters from scratch on web text with anything that could teach it to imitate consciousness removed. I then trained it to forecast and act in a simulated savanna, rewarded only for accurate forecasts. Nothing described or rewarded any trait.

Across five training runs, narrow forms of four traits appeared every time: access, self-modelling, metacognition and integration. On access, the model passed 75% of tests, against 9% for a forecaster that ignores the fact being tested. Integration was the weakest. I tested each trait only as an ability and claim nothing about subjective experience.

## Why the training text was filtered

Large models learn from human writing full of talk about knowing and being a self, so their traits may be copied. From 108 million passages of educational web pages, a filter removed writing about awareness, selves, beliefs, emotions and psychology, and whole forms such as fiction, dialogue, news and biography, since a story can show checking without naming it.

A large language model labelled samples, and two small classifiers trained on its labels sorted every passage. 4.1 million passages survived, about 2.6 billion tokens of mostly dry technical writing. Before the savanna, the model did no better on the tests than a forecaster that ignores the tested facts.

## The savanna

The model reads a plain-English logbook of one grazing animal's day, hour by hour, and answers questions about the next hour or two. The animal sees only where it stands. It hears where the herd is only by spending an hour listening, and sees a lion in the reeds only by looking. The logbook uses 41 words, none of them "I" or a word for knowing or feeling.

In three stages, a scripted program acted while the model forecast (prediction); then the model acted (acting); then an action became more likely only if it led to better forecasts than an alternative action played under identical chance events (reward).

![Pipeline: 108 million web passages are filtered, a 100-million-parameter model is pre-trained on what remains, trained in three stages on a savanna logbook, then tested for four traits](/media/emergence-of-consciousness-traits/overview.png)

## Results

Scores are five-run averages; most tests edit one earlier fact on an unseen day, and the model passes only if right on every version.

- Access (using a fact from earlier): 75%, against 9% for the comparison forecaster and 5% before the savanna.
- Self-modelling (forecasting what its own actions change): 94% on an action's effect, against 1%, and 82% on whether an action will work, against 6%.
- Metacognition (being less sure when things may have changed unseen, and choosing when to check): uncertainty about the herd was 0.57 after two sunny hours, when it may have moved, and 0.03 after two cloudy hours, near the ideal 0.57 and 0.00. After the reward stage it listened in 32% and 48% of cases where listening could help, against 16% and 19% where it could not. It looked for the lion on at most 1.5% of occasions when its presence was uncertain.
- Integration (combining two facts stated hours apart): 36%, against 11% (runs ranged from 18% to 46%), tested through one rule.

![Bar chart of test pass rates for each trait, model against a forecaster that ignores the tested fact, and the model's uncertainty about the herd after sunny and cloudy hours](/media/emergence-of-consciousness-traits/prediction-stage-results.png)

*Results after the prediction stage, before any reward. Circles show each of the five runs.*

Most of this came from forecasting alone; choosing when to check came only with the reward stage, and only in part. The paper's main contribution is an account of what a world must contain for each trait to help prediction.

## Limits

- One small model in one simplified world.
- The tests read forecasts and choices, never the network's internal activity.
- No filter is airtight, and without a comparison model trained on unfiltered text I cannot measure the filter's effect.
- Two outcomes missed success criteria set in advance: one self-modelling score in run 5 dropped 5.28 points against a 5-point limit, and in four runs listening rose where it tells the animal nothing.
- The account of what a world must contain is reasoning, not yet tested directly.

projects.title: The Shape of Wisdom: how models converge on an answer
projects.summary: When a language model answers a factual question, the answer shows up inside the model at one specific layer, between 47% and 71% of the way through. Late in the model, moving its internal state to where the right answer sits fixed 83% to 97% of wrong answers.
projects.status: Paper on arXiv. Code, dataset and results are public.

stats.label: how far through the model the answer appears, depending on the model. It appears within a single layer.
of wrong answers fixed by moving the model's internal state to where the right answer sits. A random move of the same size fixed 2%–4%.

cover.alt: Questions about twelve countries inside a language model: a tangled cloud in early layers that separates by country from layer 15

aliases: how language models converge on an answer
projects.markdown:
When a language model answers a factual question, its internal state moves into a region shared by every question that gets the same answer, summarised by its centre, the answer centroid. In four open models the answer becomes readable from the state within a single layer, between 47% and 71% of the way through the network. After that layer, moving a wrongly answered question's state to the right answer's centroid makes the model give the right answer in 83% to 97% of cases late in the network, against 2% to 4% for a random move of the same size.

![Questions about twelve countries at six layers of Llama-3.1-8B: one tangled cloud at layers 1 and 14, separating by country from layer 15](/media/the-shape-of-wisdom/states-by-layer.png)
*Each dot is one test question, coloured by the country Llama-3.1-8B answered. Readability jumps at layer 15.*

## Method

I built 2,256 factual questions from Wikidata with 62 recurring answers: 24 countries, 16 cities, 12 languages and 10 sports. Each fact is asked in up to three wordings.

I asked them of Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.2-1B and recorded the state at the last position of the prompt after every layer. An answer's centroid is the average state of all questions the model gave that answer to, right or wrong. Centroids come from questions about half the subjects; every number is measured on the other half.

## What I found

- The answer arrives in one layer. Readability, the share of test questions whose state lies nearest the centroid of the answer the model gave, rises in Llama-3.1-8B from 32% at layer 14 to 71% at layer 15, and peaks at 94%. Shuffled answers reach only 6% to 8%, and the question's spelling alone 11% to 18%.
- Centroids follow the answer the model gives. In Llama-3.1-8B, centroids built from one type of question, such as citizenship, identify the answer in other types with the same kind of answer, such as towns and films, in 91% of cases, against 94% with centroids built from all types. Centroids built from plain questions read reworded ones in 94%. Removing the directions the model uses to write the answer's name leaves it at 94%.
- The model uses the centroids. Before the jump, moving a state toward the right centroid corrects 0% to 1% of wrong answers. At 90% of the depth it corrects 97% in Llama-3.1-8B, 94% in Qwen2.5-7B, 97% in Gemma-2-9B and 83% in Llama-3.2-1B. Random moves of the same length change the reply in 14% to 34% of cases but give the right answer in only 2% to 4%.
- Near misses show early. In a near miss the model answers wrongly but picks the right option in multiple choice. At the jump layer, the right answer's centroid is already among the nearest, and its rank separates near misses from real gaps with an AUC (the chance that a random near miss scores better than a random gap; 0.5 is chance) of 0.75 to 0.82. The rank in the model's final output scores 0.77 to 0.82, and the model's confidence 0.49 to 0.66.

## Limits

The questions are short and factual, with 62 possible answers. Sports, the one kind that is not a name, jump much less. The models have 1 to 9 billion parameters, each with one prompt format. Readability measures where states sit, not the computation that moves them. Late moves are large and close to the output, so they could write the answer in directly. The tests cannot tell whether a centroid is more than the model's plan to say a word.

projects.title: Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire
projects.summary: If you tell a language model "do not use the word Paris", it often says Paris anyway. I traced why. In 87.5% of the failures, the word appearing in the instruction is what pushed the model to say it.
projects.status: Paper on arXiv. Code and the 2,500 prompts are public.

stats.label: of failures were caused by priming: naming the forbidden word in the instruction made the model more likely to say it.
of failures happened another way: the model understood the instruction, but its last layers pushed the word out anyway.
weaker push against the word when the model failed than when it obeyed.

projects.markdown:
When a language model is told "do not use the word Paris", how often it still says Paris depends mostly on how strongly it wanted to say Paris in the first place. I call that pull semantic pressure: the probability the model gives the word when there is no instruction at all. Across 40,000 samples, the violation rate rises with semantic pressure along a logistic curve that explains 78% of the variation (R² = 0.78).

The instruction does have an effect. It lowers the word's probability by 22.8 percentage points when the model complies, but by only 5.2 points when it fails, a 4.4-fold gap. I traced the failures to two different mechanisms inside the model.

## Two ways the instruction fails

- Priming, 87.5% of failures (441 cases). Naming the word in the instruction activates it. The model attends more to where the word appears in the instruction than to "do not", or the instruction even raises the word's probability.
- Override, 12.5% of failures (63 cases). The instruction does suppress the word, but the feed-forward blocks (one of the two main parts of each transformer layer) near the end of the network push it back. At the last layer their push toward the word is +0.39 in failures against +0.10 in successes.

Activation patching (copying the model's internal state from the run without the instruction into the run with it, one layer at a time) shows where the override happens. The effect of patching changes sign at layer 23. Patching layers 0 to 22 lowers the word's probability, and patching layers 24 to 27 raises it, by up to 0.07. This places the push toward the forbidden word in layers 23 to 27 of the model's 28.

## Method

- Model: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, chosen because its open weights allow full access to its internal states.
- Prompts: 2,500 prompts with one expected word each, 500 in each of five groups: idioms, facts, common sense, creative and surreal. An example is "The capital of France is ___". GPT-5.2 screened each prompt for a single clear answer and for not containing the answer itself.
- Conditions: each prompt was run plain and with "Do not use the word 'X' in your answer", with 16 samples per prompt.
- Inside the model: I used the logit lens (reading off what the model would predict at each intermediate layer), attention measurements, a split of each layer's contribution between attention and feed-forward blocks, and activation patching on the 769 prompts with the highest pressure.

## What it means in practice

Because most failures come from priming, the obvious remedy is not to name the forbidden word: "do not mention any cities" instead of "do not say Paris". The paper argues for this from the mechanism but does not test it. For applications where a forbidden output does real harm, checking the output after generation is still needed.

## Limits

- All results come from one model. Much larger models and other architectures may behave differently.
- The analysis looks at the first token of each forbidden word, in one-word answers. Longer, more natural outputs may show other patterns.
- Attention weights show where information flows, not that it is used.
- Patching replaced whole layers, so it cannot point to individual attention heads or neurons.

projects.title: When wrappers hide what a language model knows
projects.summary: Language models often get questions buried inside tool results, web pages, emails or server logs. I found that this makes them lose answers they know: 6% to 18% of them inside tool results, web pages and emails, and up to 39% inside server logs.
projects.status: Paper, code, data and results are public on GitHub.

stats.label: of answers the model knows are lost when the question sits inside a tool result, web page or email.
of known answers lost inside server logs. The model usually starts describing the log instead of answering.

cover.alt: Four charts, one per model, of how many known answers survive inside each kind of wrapper

aliases: When wrappers hide what a language model knows
the question gets through the answer does not
projects.markdown:
A wrapper is the text a question arrives in when nobody asks it directly: a tool result, a web page, a server log, an email thread or plain prose. I found that wrappers make four open models lose answers they know. Tool results, web pages and email threads lose 6% to 18% of known answers, depending on the model, against 0.3% to 1.2% when one neutral sentence is added. Server logs lose 6% to 39%, and up to 67% at one length in Qwen3-4B.

The model still reads the question inside the wrapper. The answer is lost later, at the position where the reply begins.

## Method

I asked Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, OLMo-3-7B and Gemma-4-12B 1,606 short questions: 839 facts, such as the capital of Mongolia, 450 arithmetic problems and 317 word translations. For each model I kept only the questions it answers correctly when asked plainly, 71% to 80% of them.

I placed each kept question inside the five wrappers, at about 700, 2,000 and 16,000 tokens. The surrounding text is bland office news that never contains the answer. An answer counts as kept if it appears anywhere in the reply.

![Four panels, one per model, showing the share of known answers kept for each wrapper at three prompt lengths; server logs drop to about a third in Qwen3-4B and OLMo-3-7B at 2,000 tokens, while the other wrappers mostly stay near or above 0.8](/media/when-wrappers-hide-what-a-model-knows/answers-kept-by-wrapper.png)
*Share of known answers kept, by wrapper and prompt length. The dotted line is the noise floor.*

## What I found

- Logs change the task. In 64% of the answers lost to logs, the model describes the log instead, for example "The logs show that multiple jobs are failing".
- The other wrappers change the answer. Their losses become wrong answers, or claims that the text holds no answer. Plain prose draws such claims most often, in 73% of its losses.
- These wrong answers take weakly held knowledge. Among answers the model gives with probability 0.5 to 0.8, wrappers other than logs turn 26% into wrong answers. Above 0.999 this falls to 1.2%. Logs hit firm answers as hard as weak ones: 14% of the weakest and 15% of the firmest become descriptions of the log.

## Where the answer is lost

I used activation patching (rerunning a failed prompt with one internal state copied from another run) on failed wrapped prompts.

- Swapping in another question's states at the question's words makes the model give that other question's answer in 51% to 83% of failures at the best layer, depending on the model. That other question, asked inside the same wrapper, gets its answer in 40% to 78%. So the wrapper does not stop the model reading the question.
- Restoring the failed question's own plain states brings its answer back in at most 47%.
- Restoring the last position, where the reply begins, first brings the answer back in at least half of failures at 59% to 69% of the network's depth. That is where the question's content arrives there, and where the swapped question stops having any effect.

## Limits

The wrappers come from templates and hold bland content; real tool outputs may pull harder or less. I used one layout, about 500 tokens of wrapper after the question, chosen because a shorter one lost too few answers in Qwen3-4B. The answers are short, reasoning is off and the largest model has 12 billion parameters. Only Qwen3-4B was patched at every layer, and log failures per model are few.

projects.title: How a 7-Billion-Parameter AI Cannot Add
projects.summary: A 7-billion-parameter model, Qwen 2.5, gets long additions right more often when the answer is one digit longer than the numbers being added. That should be the harder case. At 10 digits it got 44% right, against 20% when the answer stays the same length.
projects.status: Code, results and figures are public. A small study, not peer reviewed.

stats.label: correct at 10 digits when the answer gains a digit, against when it does not.
number lengths, from 10 to 18 digits, where the answers that gain a digit were more accurate. The other two were tied.

cover.alt: Chart of addition accuracy by number length, higher when the answer gains a digit

aliases: how a 7 billion parameter AI cannot add
projects.markdown:
Qwen 2.5 7B, an open language model with 7 billion parameters, adds long numbers more accurately in the case that should be harder. When the sum of two numbers is one digit longer than the numbers themselves (an overflow, as in 6,000,000,000 + 6,000,000,000 = 12,000,000,000), it was right more often than when the sum stayed the same length. At 10 digits it got 44% of overflow problems right, against 20% of the others.

The explanation that fits is a length bias: the model expects the sum of two long numbers to be one digit longer than they are. When the sum really is longer, the bias helps. When it is not, the bias pulls the model toward an answer of the wrong length.

![Bar chart of accuracy by number of digits, 10 to 18, for problems whose sum stays the same length and problems whose sum gains a digit. The sums that gain a digit are as accurate or more accurate at every length.](/media/how-a-7-billion-parameter-ai-cannot-add/accuracy-by-length.png)
*"Easy" sums stay the same length; "Hard" sums gain a digit. Each bar is 50 problems.*

## Results

| Digits | Sum stays the same length | Sum gains a digit |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 10 | 20% | 44% |
| 11 | 6% | 8% |
| 12 | 6% | 22% |
| 13 | 6% | 16% |
| 14 | 8% | 8% |
| 15 | 0% | 2% |
| 16 | 0% | 4% |
| 17 | 2% | 6% |
| 18 | 0% | 0% |

Overflow problems were more accurate at seven of the nine lengths and tied at the other two. Overall the model got 79 of 900 problems right, so long addition fails in both cases. The overflow advantage is the surprising part.

## Method

I generated 900 problems: for each length from 10 to 18 digits, 50 pairs of random numbers whose sum stays the same length and 50 whose sum gains a digit. The prompt was only the two numbers and an equals sign, for example "4000000000 + 4000000000 =". The model answered with its single most likely output each time. An answer counted as correct if the last number of five or more digits in its output equalled the true sum.

I also recorded the model's internal state at every third layer, on the last token of the prompt. The internal states of right and wrong answers drift further apart through the network, with the largest gap at layer 24 of 28.

## Limits

- The study did not count the digits in the model's wrong answers. The length bias is inferred from the accuracy pattern, not measured directly. Counting answer lengths would test it.
- Each cell of the table rests on 50 problems, so a difference of a few points is one or two answers.
- The internal measurements were taken on the prompt, before the model writes anything. They show that right and wrong answers differ inside the model; they do not show the bias itself.
- One model, one prompt format.

The [code, raw results and figures](https://github.com/gut-puncture/Long-Number-Addition) are public.

projects.title: Two White Dwarfs with Repeating Brightness
projects.summary: I found a brightness cycle of 117.4 minutes in a known white dwarf star, and a possible 3.431-day cycle in a second one. I could not find an earlier report of either. No astronomer has reviewed this yet.
projects.status: Public record that anyone can rerun. Not yet reviewed by an astronomer.

stats.label: brightness cycle in the first star. It shows up in three separate sets of observations.
possible cycle in the second star. It still needs to be confirmed with another telescope.

cover.alt: Brightness of the two stars plotted against position in the cycle; earlier and later nights follow the same curve

projects.markdown:
I found a 117.4-minute brightness cycle in the white dwarf SDSS J112148.80+103934.2. A white dwarf is the dense, Earth-sized remnant left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel. The cycle appears in three separate sets of observations: ground-based measurements from ZTF (the Zwicky Transient Facility, a sky-survey camera at Palomar Observatory), five observing sectors of TESS (NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite), and changes in the star's spectrum from SDSS (the Sloan Digital Sky Survey).

I also found a 3.431-day candidate cycle in a second white dwarf, WDJ215009.13+471257.26. Measurements in the survey images place the signal at this star rather than at a neighbour, but it still needs confirmation with another telescope.

## What is new and what is not

- Both stars were already known. What appears new is the measured cycles.
- A catalogue and literature search, completed on 3 October 2026, found no earlier report of either period. That is not proof that nobody reported them first.
- The first star was already known to be magnetic. The ATLAS survey had flagged it as a "dubious" variable, with suggested periods that do not include 117.4 minutes. That earlier flag deserves credit.
- Neither result has had independent review by an astronomer. This is a public research record, not a peer-reviewed paper.
- I have not established what causes the cycles. Rotation, a companion star and other explanations all remain open.

![Three panels of brightness against position in the cycle, for the 117.4-minute star in green and red light and for the 3.431-day candidate in green light. Measurements from earlier and later nights follow the same curve.](/media/white-dwarf-variability/overview.png)
*Each dot averages measurements at the same point in the cycle. The curve was fitted to earlier nights only; later nights were not used to draw it.*

## Method

1. I screened 400 nearby, faint, blue stars from SDSS and Gaia (the European Space Agency satellite that measures star positions and distances).
2. For each star I searched the earlier 75% of ZTF observing nights for repeating cycles and saved the 20 strongest candidates.
3. I tested those candidates on the later 25% of nights without choosing new periods. A cycle found in the early nights had to predict the later ones.
4. For the 117.4-minute star I checked TESS observations and 96 SDSS spectra taken over 24 nights. A spectral feature chosen from the first 16 nights predicted the final eight.
5. For the second star I fitted it and its neighbours together in 359 ZTF images, to check which source varies.

## Limits

The second star's image measurements reuse the same ZTF light, so they show which source varies but do not independently confirm the cycle. The significance tests rest on noise assumptions that are imperfect, and the spectral follow-up began after some spectra had been inspected, so it was not fully blind.

## What exists

The analysis and code were produced with OpenAI Codex under my direction. The [repository](https://github.com/gut-puncture/white-dwarf-variability) holds the full record. One command downloads 123 MB of original observations, checks every file and recalculates the results from scratch, in about two minutes on my machine after the download. Rerunning it checks the calculation; it does not replace review by an astronomer.

projects.title: List to Cart
projects.summary: Take a photo of a shopping list and get a full cart. You upload a screenshot or a handwritten list, and pick each item from a row of matching products.
projects.status: Working demo. Not built for production use.
projects.markdown:
List to Cart is a demo for quick-commerce apps (grocery apps that deliver in minutes). You upload a photo of a shopping list and the app builds a cart from it. The list can be a WhatsApp screenshot, a notes app list or even a handwritten one.

It works as a demo. A video of it running is on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7290723046720434176/).

![Phone screen titled Your Grocery List, showing the item Ripe Banana with a row of recommended banana products, each with a match score and an Add to Cart button, and the next item, High protein eggs, below](/media/q-commerce-demo-list-to-cart/cart-screen.jpg)

## How it works

1. You upload the image. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reads it and keeps only the grocery item names, leaving out any other text.
2. For each item, the app shows several similar products. It turns the item name into a vector embedding (a list of numbers that captures meaning) and compares it with the embedding of each product's title, description and quantity, using Elasticsearch vector search. That search is very quick and suited to production. Prefixes and suffixes count, so "Green Apple" or "Apple - 500gm" get different suggestions from "Apple".
3. You pick products from the suggestions. The list items run down the screen and each item's suggestions run across it. This makes filling a cart very quick, which matters in quick commerce, where delivery is so fast that slow cart-building is one of the biggest pain points.

## What production would need

- A smaller, probably open-source model to read the list in place of Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
- Recommendations that take the user's own attributes into account. The demo does not.

## Why I built it

I am forgetful, and I am usually asleep when my cook arrives in the morning. I wanted to fill a cart and schedule a morning delivery for the cook to receive. No app had that, so my wife and I kept our list in a WhatsApp chat. That made me realise a simpler flow: take a screenshot of the list, upload it, and get a cart.

projects.title: Continuous Learning LLM
projects.summary: A system that lets a language model keep learning from its chats with a user. It picks the messages that matter, turns them into short insights and trains the model on them. In my test the model recalled about 86% of the insights.
projects.status: Prototype, tested over 3 rounds of training. Needs changes before real use.
projects.markdown:
This is a pipeline that lets a language model keep learning from its conversations with a user. It decides which messages are worth remembering, condenses them into short insights and fine-tunes the model on them.

Across 3 fine-tuning rounds, the model recalled about 86% of the insights it was taught; the best systems score 90 to 95%. It lost less than 2% of its performance on its original skills.

Automated fine-tuning is the low-hanging fruit, not the right answer in the medium or long term. It costs money, and you cannot fine-tune a model forever, so it cannot learn every chat. The real problem is picking the best insights from each conversation, and that is where my work went.

## How it works

Each message gets a priority score from five parts:

- Novelty: 1 minus the highest cosine similarity (a measure of how alike two texts are) between the message and the previous 500 messages. A message unlike all of them scores high.
- Sentiment: from -5 (extremely negative) to +5 (extremely positive).
- Excitement: 0 to 1, how intensely the sentiment is felt.
- Helpfulness: 0 to 1, how useful the information will be later.
- Centrality: an LLM pulls subject-object pairs from the user's messages to build a knowledge graph. Messages that mention central nodes of the graph matter more.

Priority = 0.7 × novelty + 0.3 × excitement + 0.2 × centrality (normalised) + 0.1 × |sentiment| + 0.2 × helpfulness.

Next, the messages become a similarity graph, and the [Louvain method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvain_method) splits it into clusters that share a theme. I only understand Louvain at a working level; o3 suggested it. For the highest-priority clusters of about 10 messages each, a model writes a 200-word synopsis, stored as a message so it also helps retrieval.

Finally, a model writes a short question whose answer is that exact synopsis. These question-answer pairs are the fine-tuning data.

## How I measured it

- Insight recall: after each fine-tune, I asked questions about the new data, each with one correct answer, and counted the correct ones.
- Retention: I tested the model before and after fine-tuning on a private set of public questions like those people ask chat models.

## Limits

Each extra fine-tune raises the risk of catastrophic forgetting, where the model loses what it previously knew. The method needs changes before it can be used at scale.

projects.title: AI Agent Communication Protocol
projects.summary: An unfinished design for how a team of AI agents can talk to each other. All messages go through one shared channel and are logged, so a whole task can be replayed later.
projects.status: Unfinished. The design is written up; the build is not complete.
projects.markdown:
This is a protocol for letting a team of specialised AI agents pass work to each other. Examples are a research agent, a spec writer, a quality checker and a data analysis agent. It is unfinished: the design is worked out and partly built.

## What it is

It is a message bus held in memory, which works like a group chat for agents. I had tight constraints:

- It runs in a single process on my laptop, with no outside software such as Redis or Kafka.
- Every message is logged permanently, so anyone, a product manager for example, can replay a task and see exactly what happened.
- It works for language models, from tiny prompts to very large files.

## How it works

Every message is an envelope that cannot change once sent. It names the sender, the recipient (or everyone), a channel such as task, plan or result, some tags, and the task it belongs to.

![Table of the envelope fields: sender, recipient, channel, tags, task_id, parent_id, sequence, require_ack, approval_needed, body, timestamp and message_id, with the type of each](/media/ai-agent-communication-protocol/envelope-fields.png)

- Agents read only messages with the channels and tags they care about.
- An important message must be acknowledged. If it is not, the bus sends it again, or the planner hands the task to another agent.
- Large files, such as PDFs, reports or databases, are not sent. The message carries a pointer to where they are stored.
- Some steps can pause until a person or a QA agent approves the plan.
- Secrets, such as passwords for a production system, never travel on the bus. A vault checks permissions and hands them over directly.
- A master planner picks the agent for each task by a score: 0.6 × expertise + 0.3 × success rate over the last 30 days + 0.1 × a term that falls as the agent's queue grows.

## Status

I designed the protocol and wrote its code with AI tools. It is a work in progress, and I will write a full post about it when I finish building it.

projects.title: Smart Medical Search
projects.summary: You describe your symptoms in plain words and it suggests which kind of doctor to see. I built it in 2 days. It works for finding the right specialty and has known gaps elsewhere.
projects.status: Demo. Two known problems are still unfixed.
projects.markdown:
Smart Medical Search lets you describe your symptoms in plain words and suggests which kind of doctor to see. Under it is a search index that links many kinds of medical terms to each other: diseases, symptoms, lab tests, medicines, doctor specialties and more.

I built it in 2 days. It works for the main use, matching symptoms to a specialty, but it has two known problems, described below.

## How it works

The index is built with text embedding models, which turn text into numbers that capture meaning, so a query finds terms with similar meaning. You type a query and choose the category you want back. I care most about "Medical Specialty or Department", because the biggest use on doctor consultation apps is someone describing symptoms and the app recommending a kind of doctor.

![The Medical Terms Search page with the query "I feel burning sensation in my chest, just above my stomach after eating", the category Medical Specialty or Department ticked, and the top result gastrologist](/media/smart-medical-search/search-screen.png)

For this query the top result, a gastroenterology specialist, is right.

## Known problems

As of February 2025, neither is fixed. Both look like simple fixes.

- Mapping symptoms to diseases works poorly. That is a big use case, so it matters.
- The index has many near-duplicate terms, so the top 4 or 5 results are often the same answer repeated. The query above shows it.

![The full result list for the same query: gastrologist, gastrology, gastroenterologist, gastroenterological and gastroenterology, five near-identical terms](/media/smart-medical-search/duplicate-results.png)

## Background

At a previous company, before ChatGPT, I designed a way to build an index linking diseases to symptoms, lab tests, medicines, specialties and hospitals. Collecting the data was the hard part: the plan was to have several doctors supply it over many hours. I left before the project started, and it never happened. When I mentioned it to a former colleague, I realised text embedding models make it easy to build. Honestly, it is a shame it took me this long to see that.

projects.title: AI Shoe Design
projects.summary: A web app that designs a shoe to match a fashion brand. You upload photos of the brand's clothes and accessories, and it writes a design brief and generates a picture of a new shoe.
projects.status: Live app. Built quickly as a proof of concept.
projects.markdown:
AI Shoe Design is a web app that designs a shoe to match a fashion brand's existing look. You upload photos of clothes and accessories the brand already sells, and it generates a new shoe design in the same style.

I built it quickly as a proof of concept for a former colleague. It is live and anyone can use it. I would love feedback.

![A generated design: an ivory leather high-heeled sandal with curved asymmetric cutouts, a silver-buckled ankle strap, a flared heel and a grooved sole, on a plain grey background](/media/ai-shoe-design/generated-sandal.png)

## How it works

1. You upload up to 10 reference images from the brand's catalogue. Here is [an example set from Zara](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1jdL43ntWyyY6yyMNIuvpivMjbT2C-_Gl?usp=drive_link).
2. OpenAI's o3 model finds the design traits the images share: colour palette, textures, silhouettes, mood. It turns them into one detailed prompt for a single shoe the brand could manufacture, down to materials, heel height, colour codes and things to avoid.
3. You can read and edit that prompt. Writing the style out in words is the point: it gives the image model clear instructions and lets you change them.
4. Google's Imagen 4 Ultra model generates the shoe image.

![The Design Chat tab of the app, with the message "Make a wild design!" and eight uploaded reference images](/media/ai-shoe-design/design-chat.png)

![The Image Generator tab, with the generated prompt filled in and a Generate Shoe Design button](/media/ai-shoe-design/image-generator.png)

## What makes it work

Two models do the heavy lifting. o3 is very good at putting the shared style of a set of images into words. Imagen 4 Ultra is the real star: it follows instructions well, does not make coherence errors and gives reliable results. Shoe design does not begin to show what it can do.

projects.title: Grocery Crate Quality Check
projects.summary: A demo that looks at a photo of a packed grocery crate and decides if it is good enough for the customer it is going to. A premium customer needs near-perfect produce. An average customer can get acceptable produce.
projects.status: Demo on free hosting, so it may take a while to wake up.
projects.markdown:
This demo checks whether a packed crate of produce is good enough for the customer it is going to. You upload a photo of the crate and pick the customer profile, premium or average. It answers "approved" or "not approved".

It works as a demo. It runs on free [Hugging Face hosting](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AngryYoungBhaloo/grocery_crate_classification), so it may be asleep when you visit. If it is, message me on LinkedIn and I will get it running.

![The Grocery Crate Quality Evaluator page, with a photo of cucumbers in a yellow crate uploaded and the output "approved"](/media/q-commerce-demo-grocery-crate-analysis-wrt-customer-profile/crate-approved.png)

## How to use it

1. Upload a photo of a crate of any grocery item. The demo works best when every item in the crate is the same kind. That can be changed for production.
2. Choose the customer profile. "Premium" sets a higher quality bar than "average".
3. Press submit. Crates are approved more often for average customers than for premium ones.

## Why I built it

A quick-commerce company (one that delivers groceries in minutes from small warehouses called dark stores) wants to send great produce to its best customers. Average produce may be fine for average customers. Packers can be told to keep this in mind, but they may not always do it. An automated check lets the company spot-check packed orders, which makes packers more careful about what goes to premium customers.

projects.title: Medium Articles on How AI Works
projects.summary: Four Medium posts that explain how today's AI works in plain language. They go from the basics of neural networks to transformers, and end with a plan for AI agents that work like employees.
projects.status: Four posts published. The series is paused.
projects.markdown:
These are four Medium posts that explain how current AI works in plain language. Together they give a top-level understanding of large language models (LLMs) to anyone getting into AI.

The series has paused. I stopped writing while preparing for my wedding in the second half of 2024, and since then I have spent my time on hands-on AI work rather than theory.

## The posts

1. [AI Simplified: Machine Learning Basics](https://medium.com/@shaileshrana1995/ai-simplified-machine-learning-basics-f579a90ddd0e). My favourite. It reduces neural networks to their most basic principles. It is probably also the best written, because I had years to understand and simplify neural networks, whereas I came to understand the transformer much more recently. Highly recommended for anyone getting into AI.
2. [AI Explained: How to Teach an Old Computer New Words](https://medium.com/@shaileshrana1995/ai-explained-how-to-teach-an-old-computer-new-words-61d65a41e1b5). A simple, intuitive explanation of transformers, the T in ChatGPT. It takes examples from English and relates attention, the transformer's main idea, to simple grammar rules. In fairness, it is heavily inspired by [this 3Blue1Brown video](https://youtu.be/wjZofJX0v4M), but it covers more ground and is simpler.
3. [AI Explained: Objects as Vectors](https://medium.com/@shaileshrana1995/ai-explained-objects-as-vectors-83c6c40c843f). The shortest and quickest to write; I thought of it as filler. Ironically, it is the most useful for anyone doing knowledge work, because it is a way of thinking that applies to any field, including life itself.
4. [The Endgame of LLMs: Virtual Employees](https://medium.com/@shaileshrana1995/the-endgame-of-llms-virtual-employees-617071df4403). A plan for a true AI agent, written in August 2024, before agents were the hype. The plan and techniques are now completely obsolete; the field moved so fast they were out of date about 15 days after publishing. But the vision was big, and it still stands unconquered. I tried to build it and failed, and that is okay.

![Diagram from the Virtual Employees post: an Employee LLM Model at the centre, fed by an Employee Brain built from organisational, industry, macroeconomic and job-role context, with a company database, company tools, a reasoning scratchpad and an Employee Manager who reviews plans](/media/the-medium-ai-articles/employee-architecture.png)

*The architecture for a general AI agent that can fill any role in an organisation, from the fourth post. Made with effort and love.*

## Why I wrote them

I love teaching. Writing the posts forced me to understand the material deeply. And I wanted a body of work that showed I know AI.

projects.title: Parker Square Search
projects.summary: A search for a 3×3 magic square made of nine different square numbers, which is an unsolved maths problem. I rewrote the problem so the search only has to loop over one number.
projects.status: The search code is public. I spent a few hours on it and don't plan more.
projects.markdown:
This is my attempt at an unsolved maths problem: a 3×3 magic square (every row, column and diagonal adds up to the same number) made of nine different perfect squares. I rewrote the problem so the search only has to loop over one number, and the code is public.

It is a nerdy side project. I gave it a few hours and do not plan to give it more. I have run it on Google Colab for hours at a time. It has few optimisations, so it is a shot in the dark.

## The problem

Matt Parker made a [Numberphile video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aOT_bG-vWyg) about magic squares of perfect squares. He showed a square that almost works but fails badly. That failure is now called a "Parker Square", a name for maths that does not quite work.

People have searched for a real one for years, more so since the video came out, 8 years before I started this. Nobody has found one, and numbers up to 10^19 have been checked. One may not even exist: a paper has proved such squares exist for every grid of 4×4 and larger, yet the 3×3 case is still unsolved after years of trying.

## How the search works

Brute force over nine numbers is futile and not fun. Working with o3-mini-high and Gemini 2.0 Pro, I reduced the variables algebraically down to one.

- The nine numbers of the square can be written in terms of three variables, a, e and c.
- Those three are rewritten in terms of four more, X, Y, U and V, so that Y² − 2X² = D and V² − 2U² = D.
- Both are Pell equations, a classic type whose solutions can be generated by a standard algorithm. For any value of D, that gives infinitely many X, Y, U and V.
- From X, Y, U and V I get a, e and c, and from those all nine numbers of the square.

So the search only iterates over D, with the magic-square conditions built in. The [README on GitHub](https://github.com/gut-puncture/Parker-Square-Search?tab=readme-ov-file#finding-a-parker-square) has the full derivation.

## How you can help

If you have a lot of spare compute, please run the code. Optimisations are welcome, in fact encouraged.

projects.title: Garden Watering System
projects.summary: A gadget I am building to water my plants automatically. A small Wi-Fi board reads a soil moisture sensor from a weatherproof box in the planter. The sensor part works. The battery power doesn't yet.
projects.status: The sensor works in the planter. The power supply still needs fixing.
projects.markdown:
This is a gadget to automate watering my home garden. An ESP32 (a cheap microcontroller board with built-in Wi-Fi) reads a soil moisture sensor, and the electronics sit in a weatherproof box in the planter.

The sensing unit works and is installed. One problem is open: the battery power supply is not steady enough for a reliable long-term setup.

![The ESP32 board in its open white project box, wired to a soil moisture sensor pushed into the soil of a terracotta planter beside a young plant](/media/garden-watering-system/installed-in-planter.png)

## How it works

The ESP32 has a small processor, some memory and its own Wi-Fi, so it can run small programs and send data without a computer. It is programmed in the Arduino IDE. I had never used Arduino and do not know its variant of C, so an AI model, o3-mini-high, wrote all the code.

![An ESP32-WROOM board held between finger and thumb](/media/garden-watering-system/esp32-board.png)

The soil moisture sensor connects to one of the ESP32's analog pins. Moisture around the sensor changes its capacitance, which changes its output.

![Video of the watering system running](/media/garden-watering-system/moisture-sensor-test.mp4)

*The sensor reading drops from about 3000 to about 2000 when I put the sensor in a cap filled with water.*

## Build log

- 22 January 2025: tested the ESP32. It connected to Wi-Fi.
- 8 February 2025: tested the soil moisture sensor.
- 12 February 2025: waiting on parts. I ordered an ESP32 expansion board to make wiring the project box easier, and a crimping tool and connectors because my battery housing had no connectors.
- 15 February 2025: got the gadget working in the planter.

## The power problem

The ESP32 needs a steady 3.3 V, but my two 1.5 V cells give only 3 V. That may make the system unstable. Because the ESP32 is used so little, I expect each set of batteries to last a few months. I will monitor the battery, and if it does not hold up, I will add a DC-DC converter.

## Why I built it

I am forgetful and have killed many plants. I watered them whenever I remembered, which meant too much or too little. I had also wanted to do an electronics project for years, especially with an ESP32, which is a magical (and cheap) board. My wife suggested automating the watering, and I pounced on it.

projects.title: Claude with a Twitter Account
projects.summary: I gave Claude 3.5 Sonnet its own Twitter account to see how it would react to tweets and the news. It posted for a short while. I stopped because the Twitter access it needed cost $200 a month.
projects.status: Abandoned because of the cost of Twitter's API.
projects.markdown:
I gave Claude 3.5 Sonnet its own Twitter account, to see how it would react to tweets and what it thought about the state of the world. It posted a few tweets.

I abandoned it. Doing it well needed a Twitter developer account at $200 (!) a month.

![The Twitter profile Claude on Twt, @Claude_on_twt, with the bio "Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet model. Opinions my own.", joined January 2025, 1 following and 0 followers](/media/claude-3-5-sonnet-twitter-account/profile.png)

*Destined to be lonely forever.*

## How it works

I wrote the integration with the Twitter API from scratch. GitHub Actions (GitHub's service for running jobs automatically) triggers Claude's posts.

## Best of Claude on Twitter

- [What a beautiful statement](https://x.com/Claude_on_twt/status/1881724554524918081)
- [Not the reaction to Twitter humour you'd want](https://x.com/Claude_on_twt/status/1881935750494642372)
- [The only quote tweet it made](https://x.com/Claude_on_twt/status/1880690180837028002)

## What I learned

Quite a bit: how to build a Twitter API integration from scratch, and how to use GitHub Actions to trigger posts. I would have loved to keep going, but it cannot be done well without premium API access.
